svg.aria-label: Sequence of a clock request: the mmci driver calls clk_prepare_enable; the STM32MP25 RCC driver enables the gate and its SCMI parent; clk-scmi builds an SCMI clock config message; the arm_scmi OP-TEE transport issues an smc with the PTA-SCMI process-channel command; TF-A BL31 forwards it to OP-TEE at S-EL1; OP-TEE's SCMI server writes the RCC registers; the status returns through BL31 and the shared buffer to Linux.
svg.text: Linux wants the SD card clock on: the trip through the secure world
On this SoC the secure world owns the root and bus clocks. Linux's RCC driver builds gates and dividers on top of them, and asks OP-TEE over SCMI.
an SCMI clock: enable the parent first
status in the shared buffer; smc return
gate bit set; probe goes on
Why does a clock need a round trip?
The roots of the clock tree (HSE, HSI, the ICN bus clocks, the FLEXGEN outputs) are owned by
OP-TEE. The rcc node in the kernel device tree lists them as inputs coming from scmi_clk;
Linux only manages the gates and dividers below them (drivers/clk/stm32/clk-stm32mp25.c).
SCMI = Arm's System Control and Management Interface: a message protocol, here over smc.
Sequence from drivers/clk/stm32/clk-stm32mp25.c (ck_ker_sdmmc1, parent FLEXGEN_51), drivers/clk/clk-scmi.c, drivers/firmware/arm_scmi/transports/optee.c, core/pta/scmi.c and scmi_server.c.
